`spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` load-bearing here rather than a nicety.

## The client that talks to it expects it to misbehave

**`ExchangeRateProvider` is a port with one method** — a rate for a Currency pair — and
everything that makes an unreliable third party survivable sits behind it: the timeouts,
the bounded retry, and the translation of the provider's bad days into failures this
application has words for. The HTTP implementation is package-private, so no caller can
name it and no caller has to. **Pointing this at a real provider is a property change**,
not a code change; the stand-in above is reached the same way a paid service would be.

| Property | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `payments.fx.base-url` | `http://localhost:8080/mock` | The provider's root, everything below which is its API and not ours. This is the substitution seam — a real provider is this one line. |
| `payments.fx.connect-timeout` | `1s` | How long to wait for the provider to accept a connection. |
| `payments.fx.read-timeout` | `2s` | How long to wait for its answer once it has. Set well above the stand-in's default latency, so raising that dial reaches the timeout path rather than a hung test. |
| `payments.fx.max-retries` | `2` | Retries **after** the first attempt, so a provider that fails everything is called three times. |
| `payments.fx.retry-delay` | `100ms` | The wait before the first retry, doubled for each one after it. |

**None of those five has a fallback in code, deliberately.** The last two are read twice —
once bound onto a settings record, once as a `${…}` placeholder inside the `@Retryable`
annotation, which resolves against the environment and cannot see a default written on the
record. Rather than keep two copies of one number, every default lives in
`application.properties`, and deleting a line fails startup instead of quietly running a
policy that differs from the one documented here.

The policy itself, in one sentence: **a `5xx` or a connection that fails or goes quiet is
retried up to the budget above, and everything else — a `4xx` above all — fails on the
first attempt**, because a deterministic refusal asked three times is three refusals and
one lie about how hard we tried. Both timeouts are set because without them "the provider
is slow" has no upper bound, and a request parked forever is one holding an in-progress
Idempotency Key. There is no cache and no circuit breaker: a breaker protects a scarce
thread pool and virtual threads are not scarce, and a cache is a second source of truth for
a number that is about to be written onto a Transfer. Both are recorded, with what it would
take to add them, in [`docs/deferred.md`](docs/deferred.md).

**When the budget runs out, the caller gets one failure whose whole meaning is "try again
later"** — `ExchangeRateUnavailableException`, naming the pair and how many attempts were
made — and that is a different type from the one a refusal produces. The distinction is the point: a
`503` with a `Retry-After` in answer to a request that will never succeed is worse advice
than no advice, so only exhaustion becomes it. That the retries genuinely happened is
asserted from Spring's own `MethodRetryEvent` rather than by counting requests, since a
plain loop in the client would produce the same request count and the same green test.

## The frontend's types are generated, not written

`/v3/api-docs` is not documentation here — it is a build input. `openapi-typescript` turns
it into `frontend/src/api/schema.gen.ts`, and every API shape the browser code touches is
an alias onto that file.

**This is what makes the browser tests worth running.** They mock the network, so every
response in them is a shape someone wrote by hand; without generated types they would prove
the frontend copes with shapes its own test author invented. With them, a mock the backend
would never send does not compile. `frontend/src/api/types.test.ts` demonstrates it on four
drifted shapes — an amount as a string, a member left out, a currency this service does not
quote, an invented problem-type URN — each pinned by a `@ts-expect-error` that fails the
build if it ever stops being an error.

Two things had to change on this side for that to be true rather than nearly true:

| In the document | Why it is not free |
|---|---|
| The `ProblemType` URNs, the problem document's shape, and a `default` response on every operation | No controller *returns* a problem document — `ProblemDocumentAdvice` does, after the handler threw — so springdoc has nothing to introspect and publishes an API that appears never to fail. `OpenApiConfiguration` contributes the three schemas, building the URN list from `ProblemType.values()` so the vocabulary still exists in exactly one place. `default` is the literal truth: any status an operation does not name is this document. |
| `required` on the response shape | springdoc derives `required` from constraint annotations, and a response is never validated — so an unannotated response record publishes a schema whose every member is optional, and a mock omitting the balance would still compile. `AccountResponse` says so itself, and `AccountSchemaReachesTheDocumentTest` compares that list against the record's own components so the two cannot drift apart. |

input.old_string: ## Never retrying `4xx` is implemented by not naming it, and a refusal is a different failure from an outage
input.new_string:
## §28's "swapping in a real provider is a property change" is true of a provider that speaks this shape

§28 says the substitution is configuration, and the README repeated it flatly. Building the
client made the boundary of that claim visible: `payments.fx.base-url` is the only
*configurable* half. The path `/fx/rates`, the `base` and `quote` query-parameter names and
`ProviderQuote`'s three field names are compiled in, and a provider that spells any of them
differently is not reachable by editing a properties file.

This is an over-claim rather than a false sentence, so §28 is left alone and the README is
the thing narrowed: **a provider speaking this shape is one line, and a provider speaking
another shape is a second implementation of `ExchangeRateProvider`.** The correction is
worth making precisely because the second half is not a climbdown — it is what the port is
for. The timeouts, the retry policy and the mapping of the provider's failures onto this
application's are stated once behind the interface and inherited by any implementation, so
what a new provider costs is a class that speaks its wire, not a rewrite of the resilience.

Making the wire itself configurable was rejected. A path and three field names in
properties buys a provider nobody has, at the price of a startup-time contract that no
compiler checks and no test can pin, and the first provider that differs will differ in
ways a template cannot express anyway — a nested body, an auth header, a pair spelled
`EURHUF`.

input.old_string: ## A `200` for the wrong pair is checked rather than believed
input.new_string:
## "Refused" and "could not be read" are two sentences, because one `catch` cannot tell them apart

The first version caught `RestClientException` — the root of the hierarchy — and reported
every one of them as *the provider refused this request*. That is right for a status the
provider chose to answer with and wrong for the other thing that lands there: a `200`
whose body will not deserialise arrives as a bare `RestClientException` too, and nothing
was refused. The message would have sent a maintainer looking for a provider-side rejection
of a request the provider had in fact accepted and answered.

So the catch is split on `RestClientResponseException`, which is exactly the subtree that
carries a status: **a refusal names the status it came with, and everything else says the
answer could not be read.** Both remain `IllegalStateException` and both remain unretried —
the split is about what the failure *says*, not about what happens next, because a provider
talking a language this client cannot parse will still be talking it on the second attempt.

The status goes in the message because it is the one fact that distinguishes the refusals
from each other, and this path's `4xx` is unreachable in this deployment — `Currency` is a
closed enum of what the stand-in quotes — so anything arriving here is a defect and the
status is the first thing a maintainer will want.

**Not a bug that any test caught**, which is why it is recorded: both branches threw the
same type and satisfied the same assertion. Two tests now pin the messages apart.

1	# Initial decisions
2	
3	Settled in a grilling session on 2026-09-05, **before any code was written** —
4	this file is the design as it stood when the first ticket was picked up, and it
5	is not edited as the build proceeds. What each ticket settled, corrected or
6	contradicted lives in its own file beside this one; see the
7	[index](README.md) for the map from section to ticket.
8	
9	Source material for the README's architecture section. Deferrals live in
10	[deferred.md](../deferred.md); domain vocabulary in [CONTEXT.md](../../CONTEXT.md).
11	
12	Each entry: what was decided, why, and what was rejected.
13	[ADR-0001](../adr/0001-asynchronous-transfer-lifecycle.md) records the one decision
14	that shapes all the others.
15	
16	> **Verify in the first hour of building.** Two of these decisions bet that the
17	> ecosystem has caught up to Spring Boot 4. Both are cheap to check now and
18	> expensive to discover late:
19	>
20	> 1. **Hibernate maps a Java `record` as `@Embeddable`** (§16) — supported since
21	>    Hibernate 6.2, and Boot 4 ships Hibernate 7. If not, every entity's shape
22	>    changes.
23	> 2. **`springdoc-openapi` supports Spring Boot 4** (§26) — if not, the
24	>    generated-types safety net for the frontend does not exist.
25	>
26	> *Both bets won, and one of them turned up a trap — see
27	> [ticket 01](01-project-skeleton.md).*
28	
29	---
30	
31	## 1. `Account` is the atomic entity — no `User`
32	
33	No owner is modelled. Every operational requirement is account-shaped:
34	transfers move money between account IDs, and all three screens are unscoped.
35	The spec's "felhasználói számla" reads as an adjective, not a modelling
36	instruction.
37	
38	`Account` is a mutable class with a protected no-arg constructor, which is the
39	only shape JPA can map — a `record` compiles, boots and passes `validate`, then
40	throws on the first write. Adding an `owner` field later is additive and
41	non-breaking either way. `User` is named in `CONTEXT.md` as deliberately
42	unmodelled.
43	
44	**Rejected — an empty `interface AccountOwner {}` stub.** Works in TypeScript,
45	where structural typing makes an empty interface a maximally-wide "shape TBD"
46	placeholder that erases at compile time. Java is nominally typed, so an empty
47	interface nothing implements is satisfied by *nothing*; the field can only ever
48	be `null`; JPA cannot map a relationship to a type without an `@Id`, so the app
49	fails to start; and the field leaks into the API response as a permanent
50	`"owner": null`.
51	
52	**Rejected — an `OwnershipPolicy` seam.** A stub that names a rule asserts the
53	rule exists. It would read as ownership implemented permissively, not deferred.
54	
55	> The `record` sentence above is a correction from **[ticket 08](08-account-entity.md)**, which measured it.
56	
57	---
58	
59	## 2. Authentication is stubbed, not built
60	
61	No authentication scheme and no principal — nothing downstream learns who
62	called, so no controller signature carries identity.
63	
64	Implemented with Spring Security rather than a hand-rolled filter, with each
65	setting justified rather than arbitrarily disabled: CSRF off (stateless JSON
66	API, no cookies), `STATELESS` session policy, CORS enabled (the React dev
67	server is a different origin), `permitAll` on `/api/**` — plus the one real
68	rule from §10.
69	
70	**Watch out:** Spring Security runs before Spring MVC and intercepts CORS
71	preflight `OPTIONS` requests. Needs `.cors(withDefaults())` *and* a
72	`CorsConfigurationSource` bean; the MVC-level `@CrossOrigin` annotation alone
73	will not work. Symptom is opaque CORS failures in the browser while `curl`
74	works.
75	
76	> **Built in [ticket 04](04-security-chain-cors.md)**, deny-by-default rather than
77	> permit-by-default, with three alternatives rejected in the writing.
78	
79	---
80	
81	## 3. Idempotency lives in the service layer, behind a seam
82	
83	Not in the request pipeline. A filter-level check decides *before* the
84	transaction that moves money opens, leaving a window between "no prior request
85	found" and "funds reserved" — exactly the race the requirement is about. It
86	also fights the servlet API: hashing the body consumes the stream, and
87	replaying a `201` means re-emitting a response you didn't produce.
88	
89	The seam, so the implementation can be replaced without touching money
90	movement:
91	
92	```java
93	public interface IdempotentExecution {
94	    <T> T executeOnce(String key, String payloadHash, Supplier<T> operation);
95	}
96	```
97	
98	Named replacements it holds a place for: pessimistic `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`
99	instead of relying on constraint violation, a Redis-backed store once there is
100	more than one instance, or folding into the outbox.
101	
102	> **[Ticket 16](16-idempotent-execution.md)** built the storage and the claim
103	> mechanics underneath this port and deliberately left the port itself to
104	> [ticket 17](17-duplicate-resolution.md), which is the first thing with a caller
105	> for it.
106	> **[Ticket 17](17-duplicate-resolution.md)** built the port, and it takes a
107	> fourth parameter the sketch above does not: a replay is read back out of a
108	> database column, and erasure means `T` cannot say what to read it back as.
109	
110	---
111	
112	## 4. Request handling is three phases
113	
114	1. **Claim the key** — insert the idempotency row as `IN_PROGRESS`, commit
115	   immediately and alone. The unique constraint serialises concurrent
116	   duplicates.
117	2. **Resolve the FX rate** — no transaction open, no locks held. A flaky
118	   provider costs only wall clock.
119	3. **Reserve funds** — one transaction: lock both accounts, check the available
120	   balance, reserve, create the transfer and its check ledger, *and* flip the
121	   idempotency record to `SUCCEEDED` with the stored response.
122	
123	Phase 3 bundles the status update with the reservation deliberately. If they
124	could commit separately, a crash between them leaves funds reserved and the
125	record stuck at `IN_PROGRESS` — the client is told `409` forever for a transfer
126	that really happened. Bundled, the only crash window is after phase 1: a
127	claimed key with nothing reserved, ~~which is a stale row and exactly what the
128	retry path exists for~~ — a stale row that no retry can clear, because the retry
129	path is the `FAILED` one and a crash leaves `IN_PROGRESS`.
130	
131	> **[Ticket 16](16-idempotent-execution.md)** struck that clause and has the
132	> evidence, along with the propagation this section implies for the `SUCCEEDED`
133	> flip without naming it. The unrecoverable stale row is in
134	> [deferred.md](../deferred.md).
135	> **[Ticket 17](17-duplicate-resolution.md)** put the three phases in an order,
136	> and ships with **phase 2 absent** rather than guessed at: `executeOnce` opens
137	> the phase-3 transaction, so there is nowhere in the port to run an FX call
138	> outside it, and ticket 26 is the first caller that has one.
139	
140	> **Phase 3 is built in [ticket 13](13-reserve-funds.md)** and reached over HTTP in
141	> **[ticket 14](14-request-transfer-endpoint.md)**, whose transaction is the one ticket 16
142	> widens to carry the idempotency record's flip in the same commit.
143	
144	---
145	
146	## 5. Duplicate resolution
147	
148	Resolved at the top of `executeOnce`, before the FX call, so a duplicate costs
149	nothing. The insert is the test; on constraint violation, read the row:
150	
151	| Existing status | Response |
152	|---|---|
153	| `IN_PROGRESS` | `409 Conflict` |
154	| `SUCCEEDED` | replay the stored `201` |
155	| `FAILED` | proceed and execute |
156	| key reused with a different payload | `409 Conflict`, distinct error code |
157	
158	Two traps:
159	
160	- **The `FAILED` path is itself a race.** Two retries both read `FAILED` and
161	  both proceed. Claim it with a conditional update —
162	  `UPDATE ... SET status='IN_PROGRESS' WHERE key=? AND status='FAILED'` — and
163	  check the affected-row count. Exactly one caller gets `1`; the loser gets
164	  `409`. The same conditional-update-plus-rows-affected pattern recurs for
165	  verdicts and for expiry.

31	## 1. `Account` is the atomic entity — no `User`
32	
33	No owner is modelled. Every operational requirement is account-shaped:
34	transfers move money between account IDs, and all three screens are unscoped.
35	The spec's "felhasználói számla" reads as an adjective, not a modelling
36	instruction.
37	
38	`Account` is a mutable class with a protected no-arg constructor, which is the
39	only shape JPA can map — a `record` compiles, boots and passes `validate`, then
40	throws on the first write. Adding an `owner` field later is additive and
41	non-breaking either way. `User` is named in `CONTEXT.md` as deliberately
42	unmodelled.
43	
44	**Rejected — an empty `interface AccountOwner {}` stub.** Works in TypeScript,
45	where structural typing makes an empty interface a maximally-wide "shape TBD"
46	placeholder that erases at compile time. Java is nominally typed, so an empty
47	interface nothing implements is satisfied by *nothing*; the field can only ever
48	be `null`; JPA cannot map a relationship to a type without an `@Id`, so the app
49	fails to start; and the field leaks into the API response as a permanent
50	`"owner": null`.
51	
52	**Rejected — an `OwnershipPolicy` seam.** A stub that names a rule asserts the
53	rule exists. It would read as ownership implemented permissively, not deferred.
54	
55	> The `record` sentence above is a correction from **[ticket 08](08-account-entity.md)**, which measured it.
56	
57	---
58	
59	## 2. Authentication is stubbed, not built
60	
61	No authentication scheme and no principal — nothing downstream learns who
62	called, so no controller signature carries identity.
63	
64	Implemented with Spring Security rather than a hand-rolled filter, with each
65	setting justified rather than arbitrarily disabled: CSRF off (stateless JSON
66	API, no cookies), `STATELESS` session policy, CORS enabled (the React dev
67	server is a different origin), `permitAll` on `/api/**` — plus the one real
68	rule from §10.
69	
70	**Watch out:** Spring Security runs before Spring MVC and intercepts CORS
71	preflight `OPTIONS` requests. Needs `.cors(withDefaults())` *and* a
72	`CorsConfigurationSource` bean; the MVC-level `@CrossOrigin` annotation alone
73	will not work. Symptom is opaque CORS failures in the browser while `curl`
74	works.
75	
76	> **Built in [ticket 04](04-security-chain-cors.md)**, deny-by-default rather than
77	> permit-by-default, with three alternatives rejected in the writing.
78	
79	---
80	
81	## 3. Idempotency lives in the service layer, behind a seam
82	
83	Not in the request pipeline. A filter-level check decides *before* the
84	transaction that moves money opens, leaving a window between "no prior request
85	found" and "funds reserved" — exactly the race the requirement is about. It
86	also fights the servlet API: hashing the body consumes the stream, and
87	replaying a `201` means re-emitting a response you didn't produce.
88	
89	The seam, so the implementation can be replaced without touching money
90	movement:
91	
92	```java
93	public interface IdempotentExecution {
94	    <T> T executeOnce(String key, String payloadHash, Supplier<T> operation);
95	}
96	```
97	
98	Named replacements it holds a place for: pessimistic `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`
99	instead of relying on constraint violation, a Redis-backed store once there is
100	more than one instance, or folding into the outbox.
101	
102	> **[Ticket 16](16-idempotent-execution.md)** built the storage and the claim
103	> mechanics underneath this port and deliberately left the port itself to
104	> [ticket 17](17-duplicate-resolution.md), which is the first thing with a caller
105	> for it.
106	> **[Ticket 17](17-duplicate-resolution.md)** built the port, and it takes a
107	> fourth parameter the sketch above does not: a replay is read back out of a
108	> database column, and erasure means `T` cannot say what to read it back as.
109	
110	---
111	
112	## 4. Request handling is three phases
113	
114	1. **Claim the key** — insert the idempotency row as `IN_PROGRESS`, commit
115	   immediately and alone. The unique constraint serialises concurrent
116	   duplicates.
117	2. **Resolve the FX rate** — no transaction open, no locks held. A flaky
118	   provider costs only wall clock.
119	3. **Reserve funds** — one transaction: lock both accounts, check the available
120	   balance, reserve, create the transfer and its check ledger, *and* flip the
121	   idempotency record to `SUCCEEDED` with the stored response.
122	
123	Phase 3 bundles the status update with the reservation deliberately. If they
124	could commit separately, a crash between them leaves funds reserved and the
125	record stuck at `IN_PROGRESS` — the client is told `409` forever for a transfer
126	that really happened. Bundled, the only crash window is after phase 1: a
127	claimed key with nothing reserved, ~~which is a stale row and exactly what the
128	retry path exists for~~ — a stale row that no retry can clear, because the retry
129	path is the `FAILED` one and a crash leaves `IN_PROGRESS`.
130	
131	> **[Ticket 16](16-idempotent-execution.md)** struck that clause and has the
132	> evidence, along with the propagation this section implies for the `SUCCEEDED`
133	> flip without naming it. The unrecoverable stale row is in
134	> [deferred.md](../deferred.md).
135	> **[Ticket 17](17-duplicate-resolution.md)** put the three phases in an order,
136	> and ships with **phase 2 absent** rather than guessed at: `executeOnce` opens
137	> the phase-3 transaction, so there is nowhere in the port to run an FX call
138	> outside it, and ticket 26 is the first caller that has one.
139	
140	> **Phase 3 is built in [ticket 13](13-reserve-funds.md)** and reached over HTTP in
141	> **[ticket 14](14-request-transfer-endpoint.md)**, whose transaction is the one ticket 16
142	> widens to carry the idempotency record's flip in the same commit.
143	
144	---
145	
146	## 5. Duplicate resolution
147	
148	Resolved at the top of `executeOnce`, before the FX call, so a duplicate costs
149	nothing. The insert is the test; on constraint violation, read the row:
150	
151	| Existing status | Response |
152	|---|---|
153	| `IN_PROGRESS` | `409 Conflict` |
154	| `SUCCEEDED` | replay the stored `201` |
155	| `FAILED` | proceed and execute |
156	| key reused with a different payload | `409 Conflict`, distinct error code |
157	
158	Two traps:
159	
160	- **The `FAILED` path is itself a race.** Two retries both read `FAILED` and
161	  both proceed. Claim it with a conditional update —
162	  `UPDATE ... SET status='IN_PROGRESS' WHERE key=? AND status='FAILED'` — and
163	  check the affected-row count. Exactly one caller gets `1`; the loser gets
164	  `409`. The same conditional-update-plus-rows-affected pattern recurs for
165	  verdicts and for expiry.

1	# Global Payment Service
2	
3	A payment gateway that holds account balances and moves money between accounts, with
4	currency conversion, idempotent retries, and downstream notification of other domain
5	services.
6	
7	> **This README is a stub.** It exists so the work can be verified while it is being
8	> built. The full write-up — architecture, decisions and rejections, edge cases, the
9	> TODO list and production readiness — is the last ticket in the plan, and will replace
10	> this file. Until then the reasoning lives in [`docs/design-decisions/`](docs/design-decisions/),
11	> the vocabulary in [`CONTEXT.md`](CONTEXT.md), and the plan in
12	> [`.scratch/global-payment-service/`](.scratch/global-payment-service/).
13	
14	## Requirements
15	
16	**A JDK 21 or newer** for the backend, and no Docker, no database to install and no
17	Maven — `./mvnw` downloads the version it needs on first run.
18	
19	```bash
20	java -version   # must be 21+
21	```
22	
23	**Node for the frontend**, at the version in [`.nvmrc`](.nvmrc). It runs as a second
24	process, which is the price of not adding a second production runtime beside the JVM;
25	see [`frontend/README.md`](frontend/README.md).
26	
27	## Run the tests
28	
29	```bash
30	./mvnw test               # backend
31	cd frontend && npm test   # frontend
32	```
33	
34	Expect **252 passing backend tests** and **62 in the frontend**, with no Docker daemon
35	involved. The backend suite runs on an in-memory H2 database; Testcontainers was rejected
36	precisely so this command works on a clean machine.
37	
38	## Run the application
39	
40	Two processes, in two terminals.
41	
42	```bash
43	./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=dev,mock-fx   # http://localhost:8080
44	```
45	
46	```bash
47	cd frontend && npm install && npm run dev               # http://localhost:5173
48	```
49	
50	**http://localhost:5173 is the application**; the backend on 8080 is what it talks to,
51	and the dev server proxies `/api` and `/internal` there so the browser stays on one
52	origin. [`frontend/README.md`](frontend/README.md) has the frontend's own details.
53	
54	**The `dev` profile is what puts demo accounts in the database**, and it is opt-in on
55	purpose. Without the flag the application starts empty — which is what the test suite gets,
56	and what a deployment would get. Demo rows are seeded by a `@Profile("dev")` startup runner
57	rather than by a migration, because a migration runs everywhere the schema does, and every
58	test that reads the accounts table would then start from someone else's fixtures.
59	
60	**`mock-fx` is the second profile, and it is separate from `dev` on purpose** — it switches
61	on the [stand-in Exchange Rate provider](#the-exchange-rate-provider-is-a-stand-in-that-misbehaves)
62	below. Naming both is what a full local run wants; naming only `dev` gives you demo accounts
63	and no rate source, which is the right shape for pointing the application at a real provider.
64	
65	| Endpoint | What it is |
66	|---|---|
67	| [`GET /api/accounts`](http://localhost:8080/api/accounts) | Every account, with its balance and its Available Balance |
68	| `POST /api/accounts` | Opens an Account in a given Currency with a starting balance |
69	| `POST /api/transfers` | Requests a Transfer between two Accounts, reserving the funds on the source |
70	| [`GET /api/transfers`](http://localhost:8080/api/transfers) | Every Transfer in every status, newest first; `?status=` narrows it to one |
71	| `GET /api/transfers/{id}` | One Transfer by the identifier the `201` above returns in its `Location` |
72	| [`/actuator/health`](http://localhost:8080/actuator/health) | Health check, including H2 connectivity |
73	| [`/v3/api-docs`](http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs) | The OpenAPI document the frontend's types are generated from |
74	| [`/swagger-ui/index.html`](http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui/index.html) | Browsable API |
75	
76	Quick check from a second terminal:
77	
78	```console
79	$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/health
80	{"status":"UP","components":{"db":{"status":"UP","details":{"database":"H2",...
81	
82	$ curl -s localhost:8080/api/accounts
83	[{"id":1,"currency":"EUR","balanceMinorUnits":250000,
84	  "reservedAmountMinorUnits":0,"availableBalanceMinorUnits":250000},
85	 ...
86	 {"id":5,"currency":"HUF","balanceMinorUnits":250000,
87	  "reservedAmountMinorUnits":0,"availableBalanceMinorUnits":250000}]
88	
89	$ curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/accounts -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
90	    -d '{"currency":"EUR","openingBalanceMinorUnits":10050}'
91	{"id":6,"currency":"EUR","balanceMinorUnits":10050,
92	 "reservedAmountMinorUnits":0,"availableBalanceMinorUnits":10050}
93	```
94	
95	Those two `250000`s are the same number and not the same amount — €2,500.00 and 250,000 Ft.
96	That is the point of the `MinorUnits` suffix, and the reason the demo set includes HUF.
97	
98	Requesting a Transfer takes an Idempotency Key header, and no Currency — the Transfer is
99	denominated by its source Account, so a payload that named one could contradict it:
100	
101	```console
102	$ curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/transfers -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
103	    -H 'X-Idempotency-Key: 8f14e45f-ceea-467a-9c1c-7c9a5b3f2d10' \
104	    -d '{"fromAccountId":1,"toAccountId":2,"amountMinorUnits":10050}'
105	{"id":1,"fromAccountId":1,"toAccountId":2,"status":"PENDING",
106	 "debitedAmountMinorUnits":10050,"debitedAmountCurrency":"EUR",
107	 "creditedAmountMinorUnits":10050,"creditedAmountCurrency":"EUR",
108	 "createdAt":"2026-09-06T09:41:00Z"}
109	```
110	
111	Nothing has moved: account 1 still holds its €2,500.00, with €100.50 of it now spoken for
112	and its Available Balance down to €2,399.50. The Transfer is `PENDING` until its Checks
113	come back.
114	
115	That `201` also carries a `Location`, which is the second endpoint below — so a client can
116	follow the header rather than assemble the URL from the body:
117	
118	```console
119	$ curl -si -X POST localhost:8080/api/transfers ... | grep -i '^location:'
120	location: /api/transfers/1
121	
122	$ curl -s localhost:8080/api/transfers/1
123	{"id":1,"fromAccountId":1,"toAccountId":2,"status":"PENDING",...}
124	
125	$ curl -s 'localhost:8080/api/transfers?status=PENDING'
126	[{"id":1,"fromAccountId":1,"toAccountId":2,"status":"PENDING",...}]
127	```
128	
129	**The listing shows every status, not only the settled ones.** A `PENDING` Transfer that
130	appeared nowhere would tell an operator their money had vanished, which is the one thing an
131	asynchronous lifecycle must not do. `?status=` narrows to one; `?status=` with nothing after
132	it is no filter rather than an error, so a form that always submits its fields still works.
133	A status this domain has no name for is a `400` naming the four that exist.
134	
135	**Both Accounts have to be denominated in the same Currency.** A Transfer between two that
136	are not is refused with `422` and a problem document naming both, until the ticket that
137	fetches an Exchange Rate. Refused rather than written, because the amount to credit the
138	destination with is the one figure this service cannot yet compute: a Transfer stored now
139	would have to carry the source Account's Currency on both sides, which is a wrong number in
140	the table rather than a missing one.
141	
142	**Sending the same request twice moves money once.** That is what the Idempotency Key is
143	for, and it is the whole of what a client has to do about retrying: resend the request, key
144	and all, and the second call is answered from what the first one left behind rather than
145	executed again.
146	
147	```console
148	$ curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/transfers -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
149	    -H 'X-Idempotency-Key: 8f14e45f-ceea-467a-9c1c-7c9a5b3f2d10' \
150	    -d '{"fromAccountId":1,"toAccountId":2,"amountMinorUnits":10050}'
151	{"id":1,"fromAccountId":1,"toAccountId":2,"status":"PENDING",...}
152	```
153	
154	The same `201`, the same Transfer, the same `Location` — and still one row in `transfers`,
155	with €100.50 reserved once. The reservation is never reached a second time; the response is

Base directory for this skill: /home/mherczeg/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/mattpocock-skills/1.2.3/skills/engineering/code-review

Two-axis review of the diff between `HEAD` and a fixed point the user supplies:

- **Standards**: does the code conform to this repo's documented coding standards?
- **Spec**: does the code faithfully implement the originating issue / spec?

Both axes run as **parallel sub-agents** so they don't pollute each other's context, then this skill aggregates their findings.

The issue tracker should have been provided to you. If `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` is missing, tell the user to run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`.

## Process

### 1. Pin the fixed point

Whatever the user said is the fixed point (a commit SHA, branch name, tag, `main`, `HEAD~5`, etc.). If they didn't specify one, ask for it.

Capture the diff command once: `git diff <fixed-point>...HEAD` (three-dot, so the comparison is against the merge-base). Also note the list of commits via `git log <fixed-point>..HEAD --oneline`.

Before going further, confirm the fixed point resolves (`git rev-parse <fixed-point>`) and the diff is non-empty. A bad ref or empty diff should fail here, not inside two parallel sub-agents.

### 2. Identify the spec source

Look for the originating spec, in this order:

1. Issue references in the commit messages (`#123`, `Closes #45`, GitLab `!67`, etc.), fetched via the workflow in `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.
2. A path the user passed as an argument.
3. A spec file under `docs/`, `specs/`, or `.scratch/` matching the branch name or feature.
4. If nothing is found, ask the user where the spec is. If they say there isn't one, the **Spec** sub-agent will skip and report "no spec available".

### 3. Identify the standards sources

Anything in the repo that documents how code should be written, such as `CODING_STANDARDS.md` or `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

On top of whatever the repo documents, the Standards axis always carries the **smell baseline** below: a fixed set of Fowler code smells (_Refactoring_, ch.3) that applies even when a repo documents nothing. Two rules bind it:

- **The repo overrides.** A documented repo standard always wins; where it endorses something the baseline would flag, suppress the smell.
- **Always a judgement call.** Each smell is a labelled heuristic ("possible Feature Envy"), never a hard violation. Like any standard here, skip anything tooling already enforces.

Each smell reads *what it is* → *how to fix*; match it against the diff:

- **Mysterious Name**: a function, variable, or type whose name doesn't reveal what it does or holds. → rename it; if no honest name comes, the design's murky.
- **Duplicated Code**: the same logic shape appears in more than one hunk or file in the change. → extract the shared shape, call it from both.
- **Feature Envy**: a method that reaches into another object's data more than its own. → move the method onto the data it envies.
- **Data Clumps**: the same few fields or params keep travelling together (a type wanting to be born). → bundle them into one type, pass that.
- **Primitive Obsession**: a primitive or string standing in for a domain concept that deserves its own type. → give the concept its own small type.
- **Repeated Switches**: the same `switch`/`if`-cascade on the same type recurs across the change. → replace with polymorphism, or one map both sites share.
- **Shotgun Surgery**: one logical change forces scattered edits across many files in the diff. → gather what changes together into one module.
- **Divergent Change**: one file or module is edited for several unrelated reasons. → split so each module changes for one reason.
- **Speculative Generality**: abstraction, parameters, or hooks added for needs the spec doesn't have. → delete it; inline back until a real need shows.
- **Message Chains**: long `a.b().c().d()` navigation the caller shouldn't depend on. → hide the walk behind one method on the first object.
- **Middle Man**: a class or function that mostly just delegates onward. → cut it, call the real target direct.
- **Refused Bequest**: a subclass or implementer that ignores or overrides most of what it inherits. → drop the inheritance, use composition.

### 4. Spawn both sub-agents in parallel

**Standards sub-agent prompt** should include:

- The full diff command and commit list.
- The list of standards-source files you found in step 3, **plus the smell baseline from step 3** pasted in full (the sub-agent has no other access to it).
- The brief: "Report, per file/hunk where relevant, (a) every place the diff violates a documented standard: cite the standard (file + the rule); and (b) any baseline smell you spot: name it and quote the hunk. Distinguish hard violations from judgement calls: documented-standard breaches can be hard, but baseline smells are always judgement calls, and a documented repo standard overrides the baseline. Skip anything tooling enforces. Under 400 words."

**Spec sub-agent prompt** should include:

- The diff command and commit list.
- The path or fetched contents of the spec.
- The brief: "Report: (a) requirements the spec asked for that are missing or partial; (b) behaviour in the diff that wasn't asked for (scope creep); (c) requirements that look implemented but where the implementation looks wrong. Quote the spec line for each finding. Under 400 words."

If the spec is missing, skip the Spec sub-agent and note this in the final report.

### 5. Aggregate

Present the two reports under `## Standards` and `## Spec` headings, verbatim or lightly cleaned. Do **not** merge or rerank findings, because the two axes are deliberately separate (see _Why two axes_).

End with a one-line summary: total findings per axis, and the worst issue _within each axis_ (if any). Don't pick a single winner across axes: that's the reranking the separation exists to prevent.

## Why two axes

A change can pass one axis and fail the other:

- Code that follows every standard but implements the wrong thing → **Standards pass, Spec fail.**
- Code that does exactly what the issue asked but breaks the project's conventions → **Spec pass, Standards fail.**

Reporting them separately stops one axis from masking the other.

# Load-bearing, not a nicety: the app calls itself over HTTP to reach the

spring.jackson.deserialization.accept-float-as-int=false

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:payments;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1
spring.datasource.username=sa
spring.datasource.password=

# The H2 console is deliberately not enabled: the security chain denies /h2-console
# along with everything else it does not name, and the Flyway migration directory is
# the better answer to "show me the schema".

# Flyway owns the schema; Hibernate only checks the entities against it and
# never emits DDL. See docs/design-decisions.md 29.
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate

# deployment that serves both from one origin sets this to its own.
payments.cors.allowed-origins=http://localhost:5173

# How long after one outbox run ends before the next begins. This is the delay between a
# change committing and the news of it leaving the process, so it is short enough that the
# lifecycle is watchable in the UI. No default in the annotation: one copy of the number.
payments.outbox.poll-delay=PT1S

- `RetriedQuotes.RATES_PATH`'s note cut from four lines to three.

- **Data Clumps → a `CurrencyPair` type.** Genuine: `(base, quote)` travel together through five signatures and `"%s/%s".formatted(base, quote)` appears four times. content.text:
Land the work committed in the current git worktree onto the main branch, keeping history
linear.

A linked worktree shares the main checkout's object store, so its branch is already
visible from the main tree: integrate locally, with no push and no remote round-trip.

Branch to land:  (when empty, use the current worktree's branch).

## Steps

1. **Establish the state**, and record it before leaving the worktree — the path is
   awkward to recover afterwards:

       git status --porcelain          # empty, or stop and report what is outstanding
       git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD # the branch to land
       git rev-parse --show-toplevel   # the worktree path, needed in step 5
       git log <main-branch>..HEAD --oneline

   Stop here and report if there is nothing to land.

2. **Leave the worktree, keeping the branch:** `ExitWorktree(action: "keep")`. The branch
   carries the only local reference to these commits, and `"remove"` deletes it along
   with the worktree. If this session did not create the worktree, `ExitWorktree` is a
   no-op — change directory to the main checkout instead.

3. **Land the commits** from the main checkout, on the main branch:

   - Keeping them as they are: `git merge --ff-only <branch>`
   - Collapsing several into one: `git merge --squash <branch>` then `git commit`

   `--ff-only` moves the branch pointer, so it preserves each commit's SHA and creates no
   merge commit. When it aborts, the main branch has moved on: rebase
   (`git rebase <main-branch> <branch>`) and rerun this step, which keeps history linear.

4. **Verify** before destroying anything: `git diff <branch> HEAD` is empty, and the
   project's test command passes.

5. **Remove the worktree and the branch:**

       git worktree remove <path>
       git branch -d <branch>       # after a squash, -D: the squashed commit is not the branch's

entries.name: ExitWorktree
entries.description:
Exit a worktree session created by EnterWorktree and return the session to the original working directory.

## Scope

This tool ONLY operates on worktrees created by EnterWorktree in this session. It will NOT touch:
- Worktrees you created manually with `git worktree add`
- Worktrees from a previous session (even if created by EnterWorktree then)
- The directory you're in if EnterWorktree was never called

If called outside an EnterWorktree session, the tool is a **no-op**: it reports that no worktree session is active and takes no action. Filesystem state is unchanged.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly asks to "exit the worktree", "leave the worktree", "go back", or otherwise end the worktree session
- Do NOT call this proactively — only when the user asks

## Parameters

- `action` (required): `"keep"` or `"remove"`
  - `"keep"` — leave the worktree directory and branch intact on disk. Use this if the user wants to come back to the work later, or if there are changes to preserve.
  - `"remove"` — delete the worktree directory and its branch. Use this for a clean exit when the work is done or abandoned.
- `discard_changes` (optional, default false): only meaningful with `action: "remove"`. If the worktree has uncommitted files or commits not on the original branch, the tool will REFUSE to remove it unless this is set to `true`. If the tool returns an error listing changes, confirm with the user before re-invoking with `discard_changes: true`.

## Behavior

- Restores the session's working directory to where it was before EnterWorktree
- Clears CWD-dependent caches (system prompt sections, memory files, plans directory) so the session state reflects the original directory
- If a tmux session was attached to the worktree: killed on `remove`, left running on `keep` (its name is returned so the user can reattach)
- Once exited, EnterWorktree can be called again to create a fresh worktree

action.description: "keep" leaves the worktree and branch on disk; "remove" deletes both.

discard_changes.description: Required true when action is "remove" and the worktree has uncommitted files or unmerged commits. The tool will refuse and list them otherwise.

content.text:
Landed. Ticket 25 is on `master` as `e602dd1`, a fast-forward with no merge commit; worktree and branch removed.

## Spec

Both findings were real, and both were over-claims in durable documents:

**1. README claimed observation the code doesn't do.** It said the exception names *"how many attempts were made"* — but the count is `settings.attemptsPerRequest()`, read from configuration, because Framework 7 discards the `RetryException` that knew the real number. If `@EnableResilientMethods` were ever dropped, a single `503` would still report "3 attempts". Reworded to "how many attempts the policy allows", and `ExchangeRateUnavailableException`'s Javadoc now says the count is the policy's rather than a tally — a maintainer reading `getAttempts()` would otherwise trust it as measured.

**2. A "Measured" section with a stale denominator.** The design record said three of *five* scripted tests go red without `@EnableResilientMethods`; my two new tests made it seven. Since the heading claims measurement, I re-ran the falsification rather than adjusting the arithmetic: struck the annotation, ran the class — **3 red of 7**, and the same three (`recoversFromTwoFailedAttempts`, `retriesAConnectionThatWentQuiet`, `exhaustedRetriesBecomeADistinctFailure`). Both new tests stayed green, which is the right answer for tests that aren't about the retry policy. Restored the file and corrected both counts.

The third item — the stale `MAX_RETRIES` reference — I'd already caught from the Standards axis.

Verdict on the axis itself: all five acceptance criteria met, retry assertions non-vacuous, `4xx` still propagates from the first attempt. The scope creep (wrong-pair check, the message split, `fetchedAt`) is disclosed in the design record.

**Two things I did not do, and they're yours to call:**

- **A `CurrencyPair` type.** The Standards axis is right that `(base, quote)` is a data clump across five signatures with `"%s/%s"` formatted four times. I left it because it changes a domain shape you settled explicitly and that ticket 26 depends on — a ticket's worth of work, not a review fix.
- **`docs/deferred.md` has no entry for either.** If you want the `CurrencyPair` idea to survive this session, that's where it should go; say the word and I'll add it.

One thing worth flagging: three sibling worktrees are still live (`issue-39`, `ticket-18`, `ticket-21`), and `ticket-21` sits on `41c6a9e`, two commits behind where `master` now is. Whoever picks those up will hit the same rebase I did.
